summary: For ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1), build subtraction as taking away / separating from a group to find how many remain — physically removing objects and counting what is left — while deliberately seeding the comparison ('how many more'/difference) and missing-part meanings so subtraction is not permanently equated only with 'take away'. Keep quantities within 5-10 with objects the child physically handles. Introduce take-away first because it is the most concrete meaning, then contrast with addition-as-combining so the two are felt as inverse actions from the start.
misconceptions: Equating subtraction ONLY with 'take away', so comparison ('how many more') and missing-part problems aren't recognised as subtraction — the classic long-run difficulty.
Trying to 'take away' the larger from the smaller in a comparison and getting confused, or reversing to keep it 'takeable'.
Recounting the whole rather than the remainder, or counting the removed objects instead of what's left.
Believing subtraction always makes a number 'small' and being surprised that 8 − 1 is still large.
Reading 7 − 3 left-to-right as an instruction with no sense that it asks 'how many remain', so missing-number forms feel impossible.

activities.title: Take-away mat: remove and read what's left
steps: Start with 5 biscuits on a plate; physically remove (drag/take) 2 into a bin.
Watch or track the remaining count fall as you remove: 5 → 4 → 3.
Say and, if ready, assemble the statement '5 − 2 = 3'.
Point to which biscuits are the answer — the ones still on the plate, not the ones taken.
Narrate the action then the result: '5 biscuits, take away 2… 3 are left.'
activities.insight: The starting group splits into 'gone' and 'left', and the answer to a take-away is what remains — subtraction felt as a physical removal, with 'how many left' attached to the remaining quantity.

activities.title: Difference mode: 'how many more?' as subtraction
steps: Line up two rows of objects, one under the other, matching them one-to-one.
Find the unmatched tail — the objects in the longer row with no partner.
Count that leftover tail to answer 'how many more does this row have?'
Connect it back: this 'how many more' is also a subtraction.
activities.insight: Subtraction also answers comparison/difference questions ('how many more'), not only 'take away'. Meeting difference early is intended to help prevent the long-run difficulty of not recognising comparison problems as subtraction.

activities.title: Mystery removed: reason back to the missing part
steps: See the starting group (e.g. 5) and the remaining group (e.g. 3), with the taken pile hidden or covered.
Work out how many must have been removed to leave what's there.
Act out or check by uncovering the hidden pile.
Say it as a missing-part sentence, e.g. '5 − ? = 3'.
activities.insight: Subtraction can ask for the unknown part that was taken away — an early concrete seed for missing-number forms (e.g. 5 − ? = 3, or 3 = 5 − ?) and for subtraction-and-addition as inverse actions. Acting it out also counters reading a written statement as a bare left-to-right instruction with no sense of the quantities involved.

activities.title: Still-scene anchor and take-from stories
steps: Look at a take-from scene (e.g. 5 biscuits, 2 with a bite taken or crossed out) and tap/lift a flap to reveal 'how many left?'.
Act out take-from stories aloud with real objects: '5 biscuits, eat 2 — how many are left?'
Alongside a parent or partner, talk through 'we ate some — how many are left?' while handling the actual objects.
Use the same manipulatives and stories used for addition, then contrast: combining makes more, separating leaves fewer.
activities.insight: A still take-from picture and spoken stories anchor the take-away meaning and language; contrasting with addition builds subtraction and addition as inverse actions.

checkQuestion: You have 5 biscuits and you eat 2 of them. How many biscuits are left? How do you know?
checkAnswer: 3 — by removing 2 from the 5 and attending to what REMAINS (counting the leftover, or counting back 5 → 4 → 3), not by counting the ones taken away or by combining.
